Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside them, a lender can still require it.

A private flood policy can meet a lender's flood requirement: federally regulated lenders must accept a private policy that meets the federal definition of private flood insurance and covers at least what the loan requires (12 CFR §339.3(c)). Its price is not in FEMA's records.

85.0% of New Jersey's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones (not 85.0% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

Of the NFIP claim dollars paid here (1978–2026), 8.1% went to claims rated outside high-risk zones A and V. That uses the zone on each claim, not today's map, and leaves out claims with no zone.

Every zone starting with A or V is high-risk, including older numbered labels such as A1 to A30 from older flood maps (newer maps use AE for the same kind of area). Policies keep the label they were rated with, so the old labels are counted on their own.

Flood map: 11 communities in New Jersey get a new FEMA flood map after FEMA's latest report, the first on November 13, 2026. Check your own address on FEMA's flood map.

Not in the NFIP (6 communities here): Alpine (unincorporated area only); Audubon Park (unincorporated area only); Englewood Cliffs (unincorporated area only); Fieldsboro (unincorporated area only); Hi-Nella (unincorporated area only); Kinnelon (unincorporated area only). Federal flood insurance (NFIP) is sold only in communities that take part in the NFIP; in a community that has not joined, has withdrawn or is suspended, no one can buy an NFIP policy.

How much does it cost here?

Typically about $1,210 a year ($101 a month), fees included. Half of homeowners here pay between $911 and $1,750. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

A quarter pay under $911 · Typical $1,210 · A quarter pay over $1,750 · A tenth pay $2,668 or more

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus the federal policy fee, reserve fund assessment and HFIAA surcharge), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half of policies, from 62,117 single-family primary-home policies. These are existing policies, many still below FEMA's full-risk price.

Coverage in force: $46.0 billion of building and $6.7 billion of contents coverage across all New Jersey policies.

The NFIP also offers policies for renters and businesses. The median here is for single-family primary-home policies, not businesses or second homes.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 31, 2026.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy, but there is no wait if you buy it with a new or refinanced mortgage.

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageNo wait
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Standard homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage; flood insurance is bought separately, through the federal NFIP or a private insurer. Exceptions: no wait if you buy while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage; a one-day wait if a map revision puts the property in a high-risk zone and you buy within 13 months of the revision (44 CFR §61.11). To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Congress has to keep renewing the NFIP's authority. During a lapse, NFIP policies cannot be bought, renewed or increased until the authority returns. Policies already in force run to their expiration date and claims on them are still handled, though FEMA says the money to pay claims may be limited.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim), and send a proof of loss (your signed, sworn statement of the amount you are claiming) within 60 days of the flood (44 CFR 61, App. A(1), Art. VII). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster. If FEMA aid pays to repair a home in a high-risk zone, you must buy and keep flood insurance on it, or you cannot get that aid again after a later flood.

Source: floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov, law.cornell.edu, agents.floodsmart.gov, fema.gov, ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

What do floods actually pay out here?

Floods here have led to 202,340 NFIP flood claims and $6.3 billion in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2012, 2011 and 2021.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2012 ($4,131,690,177), 2011 ($648,407,379), 2021 ($366,788,986). Total paid $6,250,856,025. Totals for the latest two years are not final while their claims stay open. How this is counted

That is 202,340 claims since 1978 against 197,558 policy units in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 31, 2026.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for at least 38.1% of the 44,712 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 44,712 policies reporting one)38.1%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)79.0%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 163,143 claims paid with a damage figure)2.5%

The two shares have different bases: insured-to-the-maximum counts every single-family policy with the full building limit; the rebuilding-cost share counts only the policies that report a rebuilding cost. Homes insured for less than their own rebuilding cost can also fall short. How this is counted

The NFIP pays the cost to rebuild (not a depreciated value) only for a single-family home that is your principal residence and is insured for at least 80% of its full rebuilding cost, or for the $250,000 maximum.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies; FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 31, 2026.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

56.1% of policies here pay less than FEMA's full-risk price, so their bills are rising toward it. Median premium $964, full-risk $1,453 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$964
  • Median full-risk premium$1,453
  • Pay below full-risk56.1% of 62,117

Yearly cap: Those prices step up toward full-risk each year, limited by the yearly cap. By law a primary home's premium cannot rise more than 18% a year; some policies, such as second homes and businesses, can rise up to 25%. The cap usually does not apply to new policies, and fees and surcharges sit outside it. Bills already at full risk still change with FEMA's yearly rate updates.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 31, 2026.

Can I pay less?

The usual building deductible here is $2,000 (44.0% of single-family policies). FEMA's ways to lower an NFIP bill: a higher deductible (you pay more of any loss), work that lowers the building's flood risk, and an Elevation Certificate.

Do the same homes flood again here?

Yes: FEMA's disaster-aid records hold 50,851 damage records from homes here that flooded more than once; 5,613 records are from homes FEMA's disaster-aid data flags as severe repeat-loss (SRL).

  • Repeat-flood damage records50,851
  • Records from homes flagged severe repeat-loss (SRL)5,613

These count damage events on repeat-flooded homes, not distinct homes. How this is counted

How often is New Jersey a flood disaster?

30 federal disasters for floods or storms here; the latest was Severe Storm and Flooding (2023).

  • August 2023 — Severe Storm and Flooding
  • September 2021 — Remnants of Hurricane Ida
  • September 2021 — Remnants of Hurricane Ida (emergency declaration)
  • December 2020 — Tropical Storm Isaias
  • October 2012 — Hurricane Sandy
  • September 2011 — Severe Storms and Flooding

Only the latest are listed, newest first; disasters with the same month and title share one line, which says how many; the count covers every flood, hurricane, tropical-storm and coastal-storm declaration FEMA lists here, plus severe-storm declarations whose title names flooding, including emergency declarations. How this is counted

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Disaster Declarations Summaries. Data: declarations through 2023; retrieved October 31, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $731.0 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $2,365 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Only disasters counted in the flood-disaster card are included; their aid can still cover wind or tornado damage from the same storm. Disasters for COVID, fire, winter storms or tornadoes alone are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved October 31, 2026.
